source: Peng and Nisbett (1999) Culture, dialectics, and reasoning about contradiction - Study 1 and 2 (proverbs)
finding: Chinese students liked dialectical proverbs (those with apparent contradiction) more than non-dialectical ones. Americans did the opposite for American proverbs. Yiddish proverbs, unfamiliar to both groups, showed the same split, which weakens a mere-familiarity account.
numbers: Study 1: 70 white American undergraduates (Michigan) and 41 Chinese undergraduates from Taiwan; 3-way Culture x Language x Proverb type F(1,109)=12.45, p<.001. Study 2: 32 Chinese and 34 American graduate students; Culture x Type F(1,64)=9.17, p<.01.
limits: Chinese were students living in the US (self-selection toward liking American items; the paper notes this). Proverb preference is a taste measure, not reasoning performance. Small samples. Read from the author manuscript version.
agent_relevance: Liking for 'contradictory' wisdom is a stylistic prior, not proof of better reasoning. It motivates keeping two rules alive but gives no accuracy evidence.

source: Peng and Nisbett (1999) Culture, dialectics, and reasoning about contradiction - Study 3 (resolving social conflicts)
finding: Asked how to resolve two everyday conflicts, most Chinese answers were coded dialectical (compromise, both sides share fault) for one conflict. Most American answers were not.
numbers: Mother-daughter conflict: Chinese 72% dialectical (z=2.47, p<.05, n=32) vs American 26% (z=2.74, p<.01, n=34). School-fun conflict: American 12% dialectical, 88% non-dialectical (z=4.45, p<.001). Coder agreement (Kendall) .89 and .84. Cultural gap on the school-fun conflict still significant, chi2(1,64)=8.50, p<.01.
limits: Two vignettes only. Graduate students in the US sample. Free text coded with a scheme the authors made.
agent_relevance: Shows two resolution styles (pick a side vs find truth in both). An agent needs a rule for when each is right; the study gives none.

source: Peng and Nisbett (1999) Culture, dialectics, and reasoning about contradiction - Study 4 (argument forms)
finding: Chinese science graduate students found dialectical (holistic) arguments more persuasive than Americans did; Americans preferred arguments using the law of non-contradiction.
numbers: 32 Chinese and 34 American natural-science graduate students (none physicists). Preference for dialectical arguments: Chinese M=2.22 (SD 1.07), American M=1.56 (SD 1.05), t(65)=2.53, p<.05.
limits: The effect is modest (about 0.6 SD). Preference for an argument is not correctness.
agent_relevance: Even trained scientists differ in what counts as persuasive, so a judge or grader prompt can carry a hidden logic preference.

source: Peng and Nisbett (1999) Culture, dialectics, and reasoning about contradiction - Study 5 (contradictory findings: polarization vs compromise)
finding: Americans who read both of two apparently opposed research findings became MORE sure the more plausible one was true (polarization). Chinese who read both rated the less plausible one higher and the more plausible one lower (moderation).
numbers: 102 University of Michigan and 136 Beijing University undergraduates, 5 issues, 3 random conditions (A only, B only, A and B). Culture x Condition F(1,237)=7.90, p<.01. American 'more plausible' item: F(1,101)=5.10, p<.05. Chinese less plausible up F(1,101)=6.90, p<.01; more plausible down F(1,101)=6.53, p<.01.
quote: Americans presented with evidence against a plausible state of affairs actually judged it to be more likely
limits: Statements were only superficially incompatible, so a compromise was logically allowed. This is NOT a test of tolerating true contradiction. Samples were not matched on setting.
agent_relevance: Key design for S7: the right behaviour depends on whether the two rules really conflict. Keep both alive only while the data cannot discriminate, then let a counterexample decide.

source: Spencer-Rodgers, Williams and Peng (2010) Cultural differences in expectations of change and tolerance for contradiction: a decade of empirical research
finding: Review of the decade after Peng and Nisbett. Naive dialecticism has three parts (change, contradiction, holism). Differences appear across East Asian samples (Chinese, Japanese, Korean) and are also measured as individual differences (Dialectical Self Scale). Cultural gaps are often mediated by the scale, which supports a lay-belief account over a pure nation effect.
numbers: Narrative review, no pooled effect size. Examples cited: Choi et al. 2007 Korean change-scale correlations around r=.13; Hamamura et al. 2008 mediation of response-style gaps by dialecticism; Boucher et al. 2009 replicated contradictory self-descriptions.
limits: Not a meta-analysis; authors review their own tradition. Many cited studies are correlational. The Dialectical Self Scale was cited as an unpublished manuscript at the time.
agent_relevance: Treat the construct as a lay-belief variable that varies within a culture. For an agent this suggests a switch set by task, not a fixed disposition.

source: Spencer-Rodgers, Williams and Peng (2010) - boundary conditions and rival explanations
finding: Dialecticism and collectivism come apart. Non-dialectical collectivist groups (Mexicans) showed MORE cross-role self-consistency than Japanese or Americans, and more polarized quality-of-life judgments than East Asians or Americans. Group perception may activate collectivism, not dialecticism. Asian Americans show no less self-consistency across physical settings but do across social roles. Acquiescence is rejected as the explanation of low scale consistency by some (Schimmack 2009; Wong et al. 2003) and supported by Locke and Baik 2009.
numbers: No single effect size. Contrasts reported across Japan, China, Korea, Mexico, Egypt, Morocco, US.
limits: Details are secondhand citations inside the review.
agent_relevance: Boundary rule: dialectical tolerance is domain-bound (self, emotion, change forecasting), not a general logic. Do not apply it to math or code where one answer is right.

source: Wang et al. (2016) The dorsal anterior cingulate cortex modulates dialectical self-thinking
finding: In an fMRI task judging whether contradictory trait pairs fit oneself, dACC activity for self-relevant conflict rose with a person's level of dialectical self-belief. Low scorers showed an unexpected reverse pattern.
numbers: 27 Chinese participants; dACC activation vs Dialectical Self Scale r=.71, p<.01. Median split (high n=13, low n=14), three-way interaction F(1,23)=18.42, p<.001.
limits: Small all-Chinese sample, so it tests individual differences, not culture. r=.71 from n=27 in a region picked in advance is likely inflated. No behavioral benefit shown.
agent_relevance: Suggests holding a contradiction is effortful conflict monitoring, not a free default. For an agent, 'keep both' costs budget and should be gated.

source: Zheng, Yu, Li, Fang and Peng (2021) Cultural differences in mixed emotions: the role of dialectical thinking
finding: Americans and Chinese felt equally mixed emotions to the same ads, so the expected mixed-emotion gap was not found. The difference was in discomfort, and its direction flipped with the situation. Dialectical thinking mediated the cultural gap in discomfort in the pleasant case.
numbers: 160 Americans and 158 Chinese students. No culture or situation effects on mixed-emotion indices (p>.05). Discomfort main effect of culture F(1,313)=128.7, p<.001. Chinese reported more discomfort in the mostly pleasant ad, Americans in the mostly unpleasant ad. Dialectical scores differed by group, F(4,317)=33.5, p<.01; Chinese above Anglo-, African- and Hispanic-Americans (M about 3.93 to 4.04) and not different from Indian-Americans (M=4.07).
limits: Self-report ads study. Cross-sectional, so mediation is not causal. The mixed-emotion null agrees with Leu et al. 2010 but not with Spencer-Rodgers et al. 2010.
agent_relevance: Tolerance may mean 'less discomfort with conflict', not 'holds more conflict'. An agent does not feel discomfort; the useful part is an explicit rule for when to stop and decide.

source: Leu, Mesquita, Ellsworth et al. (2010) Situational differences in dialectical emotions: boundary conditions in a cultural comparison of North Americans and East Asians
finding: Per a search summary and the Zheng 2021 text: cultural differences in holding opposite emotions appeared in positive situations only. No gap in negative or mixed situations. A boundary condition on 'East Asians hold more contradiction'.
numbers: 47 European Americans, 40 Chinese, 121 Japanese students (from a search summary; not opened).
limits: Not opened this session. Verify before citing.
agent_relevance: Supports gating by situation.

source: Many Labs 2 (Klein et al. 2018) - replication of Norenzayan et al. (2002) rule-based vs family-resemblance categorization
finding: Large multi-site replication of the East-West rule-versus-similarity categorization effect. Task wording ('belongs to' vs 'is similar to') had a big effect everywhere. The cultural gap within conditions was not borne out: WEIRD samples used more rules in 'belongs' and fewer in 'similar'.
numbers: Aggregate N=7,396. 'Belongs to' 64% rule-based vs 'similar to' 44%; t(7227.59)=37.05, d=0.86 (95% CI .81 to .91). Original: European Americans 69% rule in 'similar'; East Asians 41% rule vs 59% family (d=-.93); Asian Americans 46% vs 54%. WEIRD moderation significant after correction but inverse of the original cultural prediction (WEIRD 65.2% vs less WEIRD 59.8% in 'belongs').
limits: Tests analytic vs holistic categorization, a neighbour of dialecticism, not contradiction tolerance. Original had about 53 East Asians in total. Authors note the original theory did not predict the condition effect that was preregistered.
agent_relevance: Task wording moves reasoning more than culture does. For an agent, the framing of the question matters more than a 'culture' persona.

source: Many Labs 2 (Klein et al. 2018) - overall replicability and moderation by WEIRDness
finding: Across 28 findings, only 54% replicated at p<.05 in the same direction, and the median effect shrank from d=0.60 to d=0.15. Effect sizes varied little by sample or setting. Only three effects (Huang 2014, Knobe 2003, Norenzayan 2002) showed WEIRD moderation after correction, and Norenzayan's was inverse to the original.
numbers: 28 effects, 125 samples, 15,305 participants, 36 countries. 15 of 28 (54%) significant in the original direction; 14 (50%) at p<.0001. 16 (57%) had d<.20; 9 (32%) in the opposite direction.
limits: Only one of the 28 effects is near this field, and none tests contradiction tolerance.
agent_relevance: Cultural moderators are rarer than the literature suggests. Do not build a cultural switch into the scaffold on thin evidence.

source: Liu, Wang and Yang (2015) More dialectical thinking, less creativity? Dialectical thinking style and creative personality: the case of China
finding: Within one culture (China), higher dialectical thinking scores went with LOWER creative personality, mostly in non-art undergraduates, against the idea that tolerating contradiction helps creativity.
numbers: N=489: art majors n=84 (DT M=38.65, SD 5.91), other majors n=203 (DT M=41.88), working adults n=202 (DT M=40.45). Negative DT-creativity link found mostly in the non-art majors.
limits: Convenience sample; self-report; correlational; effect confined to one subgroup.
agent_relevance: No evidence that dialectical thinking buys novelty. Do not expect dialectical prompts to raise idea quality.

source: Li et al. (2021) Dialectical versus linear thinking shapes people's anticipation of climate change
finding: Chinese participants more often predicted a stable trend and less often an increasing trend for global warming than Americans. A priming test of the cause came out only marginal.
numbers: Study 1: chi2(2)=8.71, p=.013, Cramer's V=.235; stable 23.2% vs 6.6%, increasing 64.6% vs 81.6%, declining 12.2% vs 11.8%. Study 2 (N=118 Chinese students, random to dialectical or linear prime): chi2(2)=4.99, p=.082, V=.207; stable 5.2% vs 0% (p=.079).
limits: Study 2 missed conventional significance and its effect was smaller than the sample size was powered for. Study 1 compares nations, with the usual confounds.
agent_relevance: A causal prime on change expectation is weak. Expect small, fragile shifts from prompts that just name a 'dialectical' mindset.

source: Morio, Yeung, Peng and Yamaguchi (2022) Of mice and culture: how beliefs about knowing affect habits of thinking
finding: A moment-by-moment rating task (Mouse Paradigm) found Japanese took longer to settle an evaluation and changed direction more than Americans. Tolerance for Contradiction scores fully mediated both gaps.
numbers: 59 Japanese and 68 American students. Culture on duration F(1,125)=5.28, p=.03, partial eta2=.041; on fluctuation F(1,125)=5.59, p=.02. With the mediator controlled the gaps were p=.13 and p=.11; mediation test F(1,124)=4.92, p=.03.
limits: Small samples. Reliability of the Tolerance subscale was low in Japan (alpha about .50 vs .75 in US). A process measure with no accuracy outcome.
agent_relevance: Dialectical styles slow convergence. That is a cost: keeping a second hypothesis alive needs a stop rule or budget.

source: Grossmann, Na, Varnum, Park, Kitayama and Nisbett (2010) Reasoning about social conflicts improves into old age
finding: In a probability sample of a Michigan county, older adults showed more multiple-perspective, compromise and limits-of-knowledge reasoning on conflict stories despite lower fluid intelligence.
numbers: Study 1 n=247 (ages 25-40, 41-59, 60+): older vs young t=10.26, older vs middle-aged t=7.97, both p<.001. Study 2 n=200: older vs young t=3.54, older vs middle-aged t=3.05.
limits: Single US region; stories read, not lived; wisdom coded by raters. Not a test of formal contradiction.
agent_relevance: Compromise-style reasoning is learned with experience and not tied to culture, so it can plausibly be prompted. The study shows no accuracy benefit.

source: Johnson-Laird and Lee (2006) Are there cross-cultural differences in reasoning? (illusions of consistency)
finding: Per a search summary: East Asians and Westerners were equally likely to fall for illusions of logical consistency and inconsistency, so no sign East Asians judge consistency differently.
numbers: No figures read. Experiment 1 only, as summarised.
limits: Not opened; from a web search snippet. Verify title and numbers before use.
agent_relevance: A null on logical-consistency judgment, which limits the claim that dialecticism changes how contradictions are evaluated.

source: Majima (n.d., Cognitive Science Society proceedings) Epistemically suspect beliefs can be partly explained by an individual's propensity towards contradiction
finding: Abstract only: analytic thinking suppressed unwarranted beliefs more among Westerners than Easterners. Intuitive cognition predicted beliefs in both. The culture effect shrank when dialectical tendency and causal style were controlled.
numbers: No numbers on the page I read.
limits: Only the one-page abstract was read. Year not shown on the page.
agent_relevance: Tolerance for contradiction may go with believing unsupported claims. It is a risk as well as a style.

source: Jin, Zhang, Shu and Cui (2023) The cultural psychology of large language models: is ChatGPT a holistic or analytic thinker?
finding: ChatGPT scored more holistic than the human norm on the Analysis-Holism Scale (which includes a naive-dialecticism subscale) and on a triad categorization task. On the Dialectical Self Scale GPT-3.5 was above the norm and GPT-4 matched it.
numbers: Ten runs per model at temperature 1. AHS: GPT-3.5 M=5.35 (SD .11), GPT-4 M=5.01 (SD .10) vs human norm 4.87 (SD .49, N=702), p<.001. DSS: GPT-3.5 4.59 vs norm 4.00 (N=158), p<.001; GPT-4 3.97, p=.344. Triad task score: GPT-3.5 .87, GPT-4 .85. Results held across temperatures and prompt languages.
limits: Questionnaire self-report by a model, no behavioural task. Norms come from other studies. Tiny SDs over 10 runs make p-values describe model stability, not population variance. Answers are likely shaped by RLHF.
agent_relevance: Models say they are holistic; that is not evidence they reason dialectically. Do not use persona questionnaires as a proxy for thinking style.

source: Sun and Wang (2025) The fragility of 'cultural tendencies' in LLMs
finding: A conceptual replication of Lu, Song and Zhang (2025), who claimed Chinese prompts make LLMs more interdependent and holistic. With eight models and more items, no stable prompt-language effect appeared.
numbers: Eight LLMs (GPT-4.1, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Claude Sonnet 4, Grok-4, Kimi-K2, DeepSeek-V3, ERNIE-4.5, Qwen3-30B), English and Chinese prompts. Exp 1 (change framing, 60 items): framing effect p<.05, language effect p=.15; only DeepSeek and Qwen preferred Chinese (.01<p<.05). Exp 2 (attribution, 30 vignettes): p=.25. Exp 3 (30 syllogisms): p=1. Exp 4 (interpersonal expectations): p=.917.
limits: Original items were withheld, so it is only a conceptual replication with the authors' own items. API models; mostly p-values reported.
agent_relevance: Best evidence that prompting an LLM with a culture or language does not reliably change reasoning style. Do not rely on 'think like a Chinese philosopher' prompts.

source: Hu, Peng, Zhao, Qiu, Hung and Peng (2026) Machine culture as an emergent phenomenon in large language models
finding: Across eight tasks in a model-origin (US vs Chinese) by prompt-language factorial design, neither origin nor language gave the human cultural pattern. English prompts gave higher contextual attention than Chinese ones (reversal). Safety tuning flattened emotion tasks into a helpful-assistant style.
numbers: Eight multimodal tasks: scene extension, scene description object counts, attribution vignette, triad relational-categorical scores, image generation, emotion interpretation, others. Many human effects came out reversed; per-task statistics not recorded here.
limits: Preprint, January 2026. DeepSeek-V3 and Claude 4.5 Sonnet coded free text, which adds noise. Not specific to contradiction tolerance.
agent_relevance: Holistic or analytic style in LLMs is not tied to prompt language. Supports building the dialectical step as an explicit procedure in code, not as a persona.

source: Abbasloo (2026) Evaluating LLM reasoning beyond correctness and CoT (SIEV)
finding: SIEV scores reasoning as thesis, antithesis and synthesis. Models that do well on GSM8K can fail to integrate a valid opposing view. Some revise only superficially and repeat the thesis.
numbers: 21 LLMs on GSM8K and MMLU. GPT-5-nano: answer score 84.4 but only 15.5% overall consistency. GPT-5: 81.4%. GPT-5-chat loses more than 40 points of 100 on GSM8K under SIEV. Using a different model to write the antithesis raised GPT-5 scores by +5.4 to +14 points.
limits: Hegelian dialectic, not the East Asian lay-belief version. The metric is the author's own and validated only by the author. Single-author preprint.
agent_relevance: A direct measurement that models often fail to engage a valid counter-position. Supports running S7's discriminating test by code or by a separate generator, not the same model.

source: Liu, Sanyal, Lee, Du, Gupta, Liu and Zhao (2024) Self-contradictory reasoning evaluation and detection
finding: LLMs often give reasoning that does not support their answer, and GPT-4 detects these self-contradictions poorly.
numbers: GPT-4 detection F1 52.2% vs 66.7% for humans. Finer-grained error categories improved detection by about 10-15 F1 points.
limits: Contradiction here is a flaw inside one reasoning chain, not a deliberately held pair of positions. Three datasets on context understanding and commonsense.
agent_relevance: Accidental contradiction is a failure to catch; deliberate dual hypotheses is a method. They need different handling: check the first by code, schedule the second.

source: Jin, Zhang, Shu and Cui (2023) - value scales (self-construal) result
finding: On value-type scales the models did not look East Asian. Both models scored far above the human norm on independent self-construal, the analytic-side trait.
numbers: Independent self-construal: GPT-3.5 M=6.98 (SD .06), GPT-4 M=5.32 (SD .19) vs norm 4.73 (SD .74, N=382), p<.001. Interdependent: GPT-3.5 5.85, GPT-4 4.95 (norm 4.81, p=.07).
limits: GPT-3.5 answered 'strongly agree' to nearly every item, which suggests acquiescence rather than a trait.
agent_relevance: Split result (holistic on cognition scales, not on values) shows that scale answers are not a stable style. Use behaviour on tasks, not self-description.

source: Sun and Wang (2025) - methodological critique of persona-style LLM culture tests
finding: The critique lists three problems with reading human culture scales onto LLMs: anthropomorphism, unclear cause (training data balance, tokenization, language structure) and withheld items and prompts.
numbers: Original study used 21 items for the social-orientation test and 12 vignettes for attribution; the replication used 60 items and 30 vignettes with 4 scores per item and eight models.
limits: Argument is partly conceptual. Critique authors also built their own items.
agent_relevance: Any claim that an LLM is dialectical from a few psychometric items should be treated as weak evidence until item sets are public and many models are tested.

source: Spencer-Rodgers, Williams and Peng (2010) - priming and intervention evidence (secondhand)
finding: Dialecticism can be raised by priming. Chinese primed with dialectical self-views scored higher on the Dialectical Self Scale, which mediated cultural differences in emotional complexity. Priming the yin-yang symbol shifts European Americans toward dialectical answers. Coping flexibility in Hong Kong students also rose with dialectical priming (Cheng 2009).
numbers: No effect sizes given in the review text I could extract; the cited priming studies (Spencer-Rodgers, Peng and Wang 2010; Ma-Kellams et al. 2011; Cheng 2009) were not opened.
limits: Secondhand; effect sizes unknown; the climate priming study (b13) found only a marginal effect, p=.082.
agent_relevance: A short prompt can shift the stance, but the shift may be small. Test any 'keep both rules' wording against a plain baseline.
